summary: Specifies an initial set of identifiers for the MPLS Transport Profile. MPLS-TP must be configurable and manageable without a control plane, so it needs consistent naming conventions for nodes, links, and paths used in management and operations.

plainLanguage.summary: Every piece of a network needs a name for people and tools to talk about it. This sets the standard name formats for pieces of MPLS-TP networks.

questions: what is a meg id in mpls-tp
subtitle: Naming conventions for the nodes, interfaces, tunnels, paths and maintenance points of an MPLS Transport Profile network.

tldr.problem: MPLS-TP must be configurable and manageable without a control plane, so operators and tools need a consistent way to name the elements and objects in the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds identifiers from a few pieces: a Global_ID taken from the operator's AS number, a 32-bit Node_ID, an interface number, tunnel and LSP numbers, and pseudowire attachment identifiers. These are combined with the :: notation and are compatible with IP, MPLS, GMPLS and pseudowire conventions.
tldr.outcome: Management and OAM functions get one shared naming scheme, including identifiers for maintenance entity groups and their end and intermediate points. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6370 is a Proposed Standard from September 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why MPLS-TP Needs Identifiers
sections.content:
This document specifies an initial set of identifiers for the Transport Profile of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS-TP). The MPLS-TP requirements in RFC 5654 say that elements and objects must be configurable and manageable without a control plane. Without one, many naming conventions would be possible, so the RFC picks identifiers for management and OAM functions that are compatible with existing IP, MPLS, GMPLS and pseudowire definitions.

It comes from a joint IETF and ITU-T effort. Notation: multi-word identifiers use underscores, composed identifiers are joined with ::, and the labels A1 and Z9 mark the lower and higher sort order of the two ends. Uniqueness does not depend on that ordering.
sections.plainLanguage: A network with no boss computer still needs everything to have a name. These names are built to look like the ones people already use.

sections.title: Operator, Node and Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
The Global_ID uniquely identifies an operator. It is an unsigned 32-bit value that MUST be derived from a 4-octet AS number assigned to the operator, with a 2-octet AS number placed in the low-order octets. A Global_ID of zero means none is specified, is limited to a single operator, and MUST NOT be used across an NNI. It is used only for global context and is not related to using the ASN in BGP.

The Node_ID is a unique 32-bit value assigned by the operator within a Global_ID. Its structure is operator-specific, zero is reserved, and an IPv4 loopback address may be convenient but is not required. An interface gets a 32-bit IF_Num, unique within the Node_ID and never zero for an interface. The 64-bit IF_ID is Node_ID::IF_Num, consistent with a GMPLS interface format. A globally unique form is prefixed with the Global_ID.
sections.plainLanguage: A company gets a number, each machine inside gets its own number, and each plug on a machine gets a number too. Put them together and every plug has a unique name.

sections.title: Tunnel and LSP Identifiers
sections.content:
An MPLS-TP tunnel is a transport service that may be provided by one or more LSPs, for example a working LSP and a protection LSP. The Tunnel_ID gives clients a stable handle when the LSPs underneath change. Each end has a Node_ID and a 16-bit Tunnel_Num, so the format is A1-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}::Z9-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}.

A co-routed bidirectional LSP adds one 16-bit LSP_Num, unique within the Tunnel_ID, used for both directions. An associated bidirectional LSP gives each direction its own LSP_Num, unique within the ingress's Tunnel_Num. SPMEs are also LSPs and use the same forms. Globally unique forms are made by prefixing each Node_ID with the Global_ID.

An informative section maps these to the RSVP-TE 5-tuple (Tunnel End-point Address, Tunnel_ID, Extended Tunnel ID, Tunnel Sender Address and LSP_ID), assuming Node_IDs derived from IPv4 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel is like a bus route that riders can rely on. The actual bus may change, but the route name stays the same.

sections.title: Pseudowire Path Identifiers
sections.content:
For pseudowires, the RFC uses the Generalized PWid FEC (type 129) from RFC 4447 with AII Type 2 from RFC 5003. The AII has three fields: the Global_ID, a Prefix (here the Node_ID) and the AC_ID. Adding the Attachment Group Identifier (AGI) gives the PW_Path_ID: AGI::A1-{Global_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID}::Z9-{Global_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID}.

In a signaled setup, each direction is a label request with a Source AII (SAII) and a Target AII (TAII), and the end point's own AII comes first. In a purely configured setup, the order of the two AIIs does not matter.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire is a pretend cable between two places. Its name is made from the names of the two plugs it joins, plus a group name.

sections.title: Maintenance Identifiers
sections.content:
A Maintenance Entity Group (MEG) is an entity that needs management, with MEPs (end points) and MIPs (intermediate points) that must be unique inside it. A layer 0 section MEG_ID is A1-IF_ID::Z9-IF_ID. An LSP MEG_ID is the LSP_ID, and a pseudowire MEG_ID is the PW_Path_ID, with the A1/Z9 ordering required. These are syntactically identical to the original identifiers but have different meaning, so protocols that carry both need different types for them.

MEP_IDs follow from the end point: a layer 0 section MEP_ID is the IF_ID at that end, an LSP_MEP_ID is Node_ID::Tunnel_Num::LSP_Num, and a pseudowire MEP_ID is AGI::Global_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID. A MIP uses the IF_ID of the cross-connected interface. With a per-node MIP model, a single MIP uses the Node_ID with an IF_Num of 0.
sections.plainLanguage: People who check the network need names for the checkpoints at the ends and in the middle of each path. They are built from the names the path already has.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes an information model and so does not introduce security concerns itself. Protocol specifications that use it may, and their authors need to describe authentication concerns and how to address them.

Uniqueness is guaranteed by whoever assigns the values, for example IANA for ASNs and the operator for Node_IDs and IF_Nums. If an assigner reuses values within the scope, operational problems can follow; a non-unique MEP value could cause a mis-merged LSP to go undetected. Specifications using these identifiers need to consider guessable identifiers and SHOULD advise on making them less guessable where that matters.
sections.plainLanguage: If two kids get the same name tag, the teacher can mix them up. So whoever hands out names must make sure none repeat.

items.title: Global_ID
items.text: 32 bits, derived from the operator's 4-octet AS number.

items.title: Node_ID
items.text: 32 bits, assigned by the operator within a Global_ID; zero is reserved.

items.title: LSP_Num
items.text: 16 bits, scoped by the Tunnel_ID or the ingress Tunnel_Num.
